n: A national lament begins with memory. The people recall stories their ancestors passed down about God’s mighty acts long ago.
God drove out the Canaanite nations and planted Israel in the land like a gardener planting a vine.

f.g: The nations — here the Canaanite peoples.

n: Israel didn’t win the land by their own weapons. It was God’s power and the light of his face — his favor — that gave it to them.

f.w: not the land in possession by their own sword

n: Speaking for the nation, the leader declares God his king and asks him to order victories for Jacob, that is, Israel.

f.g: Another name for the nation of Israel, descended from Jacob.

n: With God’s power and name, Israel can push back any enemy.
The speaker refuses to rely on his own bow or sword.
It has always been God who saved them and embarrassed their enemies.
So their boast is in God all day long. A “Selah” marks a pause before everything changes.

f.g: A musical or liturgical marker, possibly a pause.

n: “But now” — the shock: God seems to have abandoned them and no longer marches with their armies.

f.w: goest not forth with our armies

n: They retreat before enemies, who plunder them freely.
They feel like sheep set aside for slaughter and scattered among foreign nations. This may reflect a time of military defeat or exile.
It feels as if God sold his people for nothing — as if they were worthless to him.

f.w: Thou sellest thy people for nought

n: Neighboring nations mock and laugh at them.
Israel’s name has become a proverb of failure, and people shake their heads at them in contempt.

f.g: A saying used to mock someone.

n: The speaker can’t escape his disgrace; shame covers his face all the time.
It comes from the insults of those who mock God and from enemies bent on revenge.
The heart of the lament: this happened even though we have stayed faithful to your covenant. Their suffering is not punishment for unfaithfulness, which makes it so hard to understand.

f.w: neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant
f.g: Unlike many laments, this one claims innocence — the problem of righteous suffering.

n: They haven’t turned away in heart or strayed from God’s path.
Even when God crushed them in a desolate place haunted by wild animals and covered them in deep darkness, they stayed loyal.
If they had forgotten God or prayed to foreign gods...
...wouldn’t God know? He sees the secrets of every heart. They are confident in their sincerity.

f.w: he knoweth the secrets of the heart

n: Their suffering comes because of their loyalty to God. Paul quoted this verse to say that nothing — not even such suffering — can separate us from Christ’s love.

f.w: we are counted as sheep for the slaughter

n: A bold cry: “Wake up, Lord! Why are you sleeping?” The Psalms let God’s people speak this honestly.
Why do you hide your face and forget our suffering?
They lie flat on the ground, utterly humbled.

f.w: our belly cleaveth unto the earth
f.g: Lying face down in the dust — total defeat and grief.

n: The final plea rests not on their merit but on God’s loyal love: rise up and redeem us.

f.g: Because of your ḥesed — your faithful covenant love.
